title: Urban Flood Nowcasting System (Drainage and Rainfall Coupling)
department: National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF)
description:
Urban flooding in major Indian metros like Mumbai, Delhi, and Chennai has become an annual crisis. Traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models fall short because knowing how much rain will fall does not automatically translate into knowing where the streets will flood.Urban flooding is a hyper-local phenomenon dictated by micro-topography, concrete imperviousness, and heavily strained, invisible drainage networks. Currently, municipal bodies lack real-time, street-level predictive systems. Consequently, cities are caught off guard by rapid water accumulation, leading to severe traffic gridlocks, economic disruption, and loss of life.
The challenge is to design a high-resolution, real-time Urban Flood Nowcasting System (0–3 hour lead time) capable of predicting street-level inundation before it happens.
Participants must move away from isolated weather models and instead build a coupled framework. This system must fuse real-time rainfall nowcasts with high-resolution Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and a graph-based mathematical model of the city’s underground drainage network. By mapping how water flows, accumulates, and surcharges across concrete surfaces and drainage nodes, the solution should pinpoint exactly which streets or intersections will flood.Develop a pipeline that takes high-resolution rainfall nowcasts (from Doppler Weather Radars) and instantly routes that volume across a 2D surface terrain model. Represent the city's stormwater drain network as a directed graph (nodes as manholes/inlets, edges as pipes/canals). The model must calculate hydraulic capacity and predict where blockages or overcapacity will cause backflow onto the streets. A dynamic, web-based GIS dashboard showing real-time, street-by-street flooding projections (e.g., water depth estimations in centimeters) with a 0–3 hour forward-looking window.An API utility that can interface with navigation maps to suggest flood-safe alternative routes for emergency services, public transit, and commuters during heavy downpours.
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on predictive, gis applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (4/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on api, gis, model. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 21/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: Urban Flood Nowcasting System (Drainage and Rainfall Coupling)

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that predicts exactly which streets will flood in the next 0-3 hours by combining rainfall forecasts with real city drainage network models and elevation data, instead of just predicting how much rain will fall.
overview.why_it_matters: Knowing rainfall totals doesn't tell you where the water will actually pool. Street-level prediction is what turns a rain forecast into something a city can actually use to warn people and reroute traffic.
pain_points: Rainfall forecasts don't translate directly into knowledge of where streets will actually flood.
Urban flooding is dictated by micro-topography and strained drainage networks that generic weather models ignore.
Municipal bodies lack real-time, street-level predictive systems, leaving cities caught off guard.
overview.background: Major Indian cities face annual urban flooding crises, but traditional weather models don't capture the hyper-local, drainage-dependent nature of street-level flooding, leaving municipalities without genuine predictive capability.
overview.whats_being_asked: A coupled, real-time Urban Flood Nowcasting System (0-3 hour lead time) fusing rainfall nowcasts with high-resolution Digital Elevation Models and a graph-based model of the city's drainage network to predict street-level inundation.
expected_solution: Street-level inundation prediction with 0-3 hour lead time.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Coupling rainfall nowcasting with a genuine graph-based hydraulic drainage network model for street-level prediction is a real, sophisticated urban hydrology and ML integration challenge.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires DEM processing, drainage network graph modeling, and rainfall-runoff coupling together, substantial cross-domain technical depth (hydrology plus ML plus GIS).

competitive_landscape.note: Genuine urban hydrology plus ML integration is a specialized combination, most teams will lack real drainage network data access for a specific city.

innovation.note: Genuine coupling of rainfall nowcasting with drainage-network hydraulic modeling for street-level prediction, real cross-domain sophistication.

invention.note: DEM processing, graph-based drainage modeling, and rainfall-runoff coupling together is substantial technical breadth.

technical_feasibility.note: Public DEM data exists, but real drainage network infrastructure data for a specific city is often not publicly available, this is the core resourcing challenge.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly addresses a recurring, severe urban crisis (traffic gridlock, economic disruption, loss of life) with clear, relatable stakes.

architecture.note: Rainfall model, terrain model, and drainage network graph all need to interact correctly, genuine architectural complexity.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with GIS/hydrology background, but real drainage network infrastructure data is the key resourcing constraint, since it's often not publicly available for Indian cities. Build a credible, simplified drainage-flow approximation using terrain and land-use data if actual network data isn't accessible.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Extremely well-articulated, relatable real-world problem (annual urban flooding crises in named cities) makes the impact case immediately compelling.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Real underground drainage network data for a specific Indian city is often not publicly available, without it, the 'graph-based drainage network' component needs a credible, honestly-scoped approximation.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm what drainage/infrastructure data is actually accessible for your chosen test city, and be prepared to build a terrain-and-land-use-based flow approximation if real drainage network data isn't available, rather than claiming a graph model you don't actually have underlying data for.

idea_0_4: Choose a test city and confirm what data is actually accessible: public DEM data almost certainly, drainage network data less certainly.
If real drainage data isn't accessible, design a terrain-and-imperviousness-based flow accumulation approximation as your practical alternative.
Split: one person on rainfall nowcast integration, one on the terrain/drainage flow modeling.
prototype_4_22: Build your DEM-based terrain model for your test city area.
Build your flow/drainage model, either from real network data if accessible, or a terrain-based flow-accumulation approximation if not.
Start integrating rainfall nowcast data as input to your flow model.
integration_22_30: Connect rainfall input, terrain model, and flow/drainage logic into one street-level inundation prediction pipeline.
Test against a real historical flooding event in your test city if documented data allows, comparing predicted flood-prone areas against actual reported flooding locations.
polish_30_36: Build a clear street-level map visualization showing predicted inundation zones.
Rehearse being explicit about your drainage-modeling approach, real network data versus terrain-based approximation, whichever you used.
Prepare to discuss what real drainage infrastructure data access would add to your model's accuracy.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: If you can validate against a real, documented historical flooding event in your test city (many major floods are well-reported with specific flooded locations), show your model correctly flagging those actual flood-prone streets, that concrete validation against real outcomes is powerful evidence.

strengths: Extremely relatable, well-articulated real-world problem with named cities makes the impact case immediately compelling.
Public DEM/terrain data is genuinely accessible even where drainage network data isn't.
weaknesses: Real underground drainage network data is often not publicly available for Indian cities, a genuine resourcing constraint.
Requires genuine cross-domain expertise (hydrology, GIS, ML) together, a demanding combination.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Weight toward GIS/hydrology skill, that's the more specialized, harder-to-find expertise this PS needs.
team_fit.approach: Confirm your test city's data accessibility (DEM certain, drainage network uncertain) before committing to a specific modeling approach.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard DEM processing and flow-accumulation algorithm implementation using established GIS techniques.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly modeling how urban drainage actually behaves, especially where real network data isn't available and a terrain-based approximation must stand in, that requires real hydrology understanding to be credible.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded 'graph-based drainage model' without real underlying network data, presented as if genuinely modeling the drainage infrastructure, would misrepresent what's actually been built, honesty about the approximation is important here.

data_resource_availability.status: Public DEM/terrain data is genuinely accessible for most Indian cities; real underground drainage network infrastructure data is often not publicly available, a genuine constraint.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Build a terrain-and-land-use-based flow accumulation model as an honest approximation when real drainage network data isn't accessible, clearly labeled as such rather than claimed to be a full drainage network model.

judge_qna.question: Do you have access to real drainage network data for your test city, or is this an approximation?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct about your actual data source, if using a terrain-based flow approximation rather than real drainage infrastructure data, explain that clearly and what a real network-data-informed version would additionally capture.
judge_qna.follow_up: How would your predictions change with access to real drainage network data?

judge_qna.question: Did you validate this against any real historical flooding event in your test city?
judge_qna.strong_answer: If you tested against a documented real flood event, present that comparison directly, if not, be honest that validation against real historical flood-extent data is the necessary next step.
judge_qna.follow_up: What specific streets or areas did your model predict correctly or incorrectly?
